After we disclosed
PHP2Shell , we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java.
Today, we are disclosing Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is the most popular Java runtime. Under CVSS 4.0, this vulnerability scores 9.2 out of 10 (CRITICAL).
While PHP is a high-level web technology, Java sits much deeper. Java is the world's
third most popular programming language , powering
90% of Fortune 500 companies . It is the beating heart of the modern economy. Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems.
Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages. What Memos does and what it needs
Memos is a self-hosted note-taking app built around a personal timeline. Each memo is timestamped, Markdown-capable, and taggable, so short thoughts and longer entries live in one searchable stream. You control visibility per memo: private, shared with specific users, or public on the web. The app ships as a single Go binary with an embedded SQLite store by default, which makes it one of the lighter services to run on a VPS.
The upstream project does not publish a minimum RAM figure. Practical sizing depends on workload: an idle instance with a handful of users and a few thousand memos runs comfortably in a small container, while heavy attachment uploads, large media libraries, and many concurrent users push memory and disk usage up. Watch the volume size more than the RAM line.
Everything Memos keeps lives under
/var/opt/memos
inside the container. That directory holds the SQLite database, uploaded attachments, and generated thumbnails. Back it up as a unit.

Fix WordPress Critical Error After Update
# wordpress
# php
# webdev
# tutorial
A WordPress critical error after update is rarely a mystery for long, but the screen itself tells you nothing. Since WordPress 5.2 the core fatal error handler catches the PHP crash, prints a polite white page, and emails the admin a recovery link, deliberately withholding the file and line that would identify the culprit. This tutorial compares the three realistic recovery routes, then implements the one worth keeping: read the fatal from
wp-content/debug.log , get back into
wp-admin
through recovery mode, and roll the offending plugin or theme back with WP-CLI. It finishes with a small mu-plugin that emails you the file and line the moment the next update fails.
You need file or SSH access to the install (SFTP covers the first half), WP-CLI 2.7 or newer for the rollback, and access to the admin email inbox on that site.
The critical error screen is a symptom, not a diagnosis
When PHP hits an uncaught fatal, WordPress runs
WP_Fatal_Error_Handler
on shutdown. That handler checks whether the error came from a plugin or theme file, pauses the offending extension for the current session, sends the recovery-mode email, and renders the generic template. Cloudflare Block AI Bots: What to Block, What to Allow
# cloudflare
# seo
# ai
# webdev
Cloudflare will happily block AI bots for you. The question is which ones. "AI bot" covers three different jobs: crawlers that collect text to train future models, crawlers that build an AI search index, and fetchers that open one page because a person just asked ChatGPT or Claude about it. Block all three and you're out of the training sets, but you've also vanished from the AI answers that now send real visitors.
I ran the same request against two sites behind Cloudflare, changing only the bot name, to see what each setting actually does. Below are the results, the current dashboard path (it moved in 2026), and what I'd pick for a business site or a blog.
The short answer
Block training bots
(GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot, Bytespider, Google-Extended) if you don't want your content in future models. They send you no visitors.
Allow AI search bots
(OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot). OpenAI's docs say sites that opt out of OAI-SearchBot "will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers".
Allow user agents
(ChatGPT-User, Claude-User, Perplexity-User). Block them and "summarise this link" fails for anyone who pastes your URL.

CAIRN uses an Observe, Orient, Decide, Act loop with agents sharing a blackboard. CyberStrikeAI connects models to security tools and attack recipes. HexStrike AI exposes many offensive utilities through Model Context Protocol integration.

Watch the volume size more than the RAM line.

/var/opt/memos
inside the container. That directory holds the SQLite database, uploaded attachments, and generated thumbnails. Back it up as a unit.

Fix WordPress Critical Error After Update
# wordpress
# php
# webdev
# tutorial
A WordPress critical error after update is rarely a mystery for long, but the screen itself tells you nothing. Since WordPress 5.2 the core fatal error handler catches the PHP crash, prints a polite white page, and emails the admin a recovery link, deliberately withholding the file and line that would identify the culprit. This tutorial compares the three realistic recovery routes, then implements the one worth keeping: read the fatal from
wp-content/debug.log , get back into
wp-admin
through recovery mode, and roll the offending plugin or theme back with WP-CLI. It finishes with a small mu-plugin that emails you the file and line the moment the next update fails.
You need file or SSH access to the install (SFTP covers the first half), WP-CLI 2.7 or newer for the rollback, and access to the admin email inbox on that site.
The critical error screen is a symptom, not a diagnosis
When PHP hits an uncaught fatal, WordPress runs
WP_Fatal_Error_Handler
on shutdown. That handler checks whether the error came from a plugin or theme file, pauses the offending extension for the current session, sends the recovery-mode email, and renders the generic template. What Memos does and what it needs
Memos is a self-hosted note-taking app built around a personal timeline. Each memo is timestamped, Markdown-capable, and taggable, so short thoughts and longer entries live in one searchable stream. You control visibility per memo: private, shared with specific users, or public on the web. The app ships as a single Go binary with an embedded SQLite store by default, which makes it one of the lighter services to run on a VPS.
The upstream project does not publish a minimum RAM figure. Practical sizing depends on workload: an idle instance with a handful of users and a few thousand memos runs comfortably in a small container, while heavy attachment uploads, large media libraries, and many concurrent users push memory and disk usage up. Watch the volume size more than the RAM line.
Everything Memos keeps lives under
/var/opt/memos
inside the container. That directory holds the SQLite database, uploaded attachments, and generated thumbnails. Back it up as a unit.

Fix WordPress Critical Error After Update
# wordpress
# php
# webdev
# tutorial
A WordPress critical error after update is rarely a mystery for long, but the screen itself tells you nothing. Since WordPress 5.2 the core fatal error handler catches the PHP crash, prints a polite white page, and emails the admin a recovery link, deliberately withholding the file and line that would identify the culprit. This tutorial compares the three realistic recovery routes, then implements the one worth keeping: read the fatal from
wp-content/debug.log , get back into
wp-admin
through recovery mode, and roll the offending plugin or theme back with WP-CLI. It finishes with a small mu-plugin that emails you the file and line the moment the next update fails.
You need file or SSH access to the install (SFTP covers the first half), WP-CLI 2.7 or newer for the rollback, and access to the admin email inbox on that site.
The critical error screen is a symptom, not a diagnosis
When PHP hits an uncaught fatal, WordPress runs
WP_Fatal_Error_Handler
on shutdown. That handler checks whether the error came from a plugin or theme file, pauses the offending extension for the current session, sends the recovery-mode email, and renders the generic template. Cloudflare Block AI Bots: What to Block, What to Allow
# cloudflare
# seo
# ai
# webdev
Cloudflare will happily block AI bots for you. The question is which ones. "AI bot" covers three different jobs: crawlers that collect text to train future models, crawlers that build an AI search index, and fetchers that open one page because a person just asked ChatGPT or Claude about it. Block all three and you're out of the training sets, but you've also vanished from the AI answers that now send real visitors.
I ran the same request against two sites behind Cloudflare, changing only the bot name, to see what each setting actually does. Below are the results, the current dashboard path (it moved in 2026), and what I'd pick for a business site or a blog.
The short answer
Block training bots
(GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot, Bytespider, Google-Extended) if you don't want your content in future models. They send you no visitors.
Allow AI search bots
(OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot). OpenAI's docs say sites that opt out of OAI-SearchBot "will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers".
Allow user agents
(ChatGPT-User, Claude-User, Perplexity-User). Block them and "summarise this link" fails for anyone who pastes your URL.

final_briefs.title: Java4Shell: Critical RCE in OpenJDK’s Base64 Decoder (CVE‑2026‑114938)
final_briefs.description: **A memory‑corruption bug in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder lets an unauthenticated attacker execute code on any Java service that decodes untrusted data.** The flaw, tracked as CVE‑2026‑114938, corrupts heap memory when malformed Base64 input is processed with the optimized x86‑64 instruction path. Exploitation can read memory (a “Heartbleed‑style” leak) and achieve remote code execution, earning a CVSS 9.2 critical rating. Because OpenJDK powers the majority of Java workloads—including 90 % of Fortune 500 companies—any backend that decodes Base64 is at risk until the runtime is patched.

The open‑source edition is MPL‑2.0, while Talos Enterprise adds FIPS 140‑3 compliance, CVE SLAs, and indemnity for regulated environments.
